title: The Most Insane Kings and Queens in History
description:
A self-declared Emperor of the United States, a tsar who taxed beards and pulled teeth, a king who heard the same four songs every night for ten years, a queen who crossed Spain with her husband's coffin, a king and a (legendary) oak tree, a king who went broke building fairytale castles, and a king who believed he was made of glass: seven of history's most insane rulers, counted down from seven to one. Several of them were truly ill, so we laugh at the situations, never at the people, and we flag the legends. Chapters are added automatically.

#history #kings #queens #funnyhistory #historypros
youtube_title: The Most Insane Kings and Queens in History

beats.say: Paris, the 1390s. The King of France is walking very, very carefully through his own palace.
Iron rods are sewn into his clothes. Why? Because the king believes his body is made of glass.
Stay back! Nobody touch me, or I'll shatter!
Of course, Your Majesty. We'll all just stand over here.
History is full of rulers like him: kings and queens who did things that sound completely insane.
One quick note. Several of these rulers were truly ill, and back then nobody knew how to help them. So we laugh at the wild situations, never at sick people.
Today we count down seven of the most insane kings and queens in history. And number seven wasn't even a real king.

show.text: The Most Insane Kings and Queens in History
show.sub: Seven rulers. All real. Completely bonkers.

show.title: The Emperor of the United States

beats.say: Number seven: Joshua Norton, Emperor of the United States. Yes, America once had an emperor. Sort of.
Norton was a businessman who got rich in San Francisco during the Gold Rush, when thousands of people raced to California to dig for gold.
In 1852 he tried to buy up all the rice in town, to control the price. Then more rice ships arrived, prices crashed, and he lost everything.
So in 1859, he wrote to a local newspaper, and it printed his letter, mostly as a joke.
I, Joshua Norton, declare and proclaim myself Emperor of these United States.

show.text: I, Joshua Norton... declare and proclaim myself Emperor of these U.S.
show.who: Joshua Norton, letter in the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, September 17, 1859

beats.say: A few weeks later, he abolished Congress. Congress ignored him. But San Francisco played along.
He wore a blue army uniform with gold shoulder pieces, and a tall hat with a peacock feather.
He even printed his own money, and some local businesses accepted it.
That's fifty cents, Your Majesty.
Put it on the empire.
Today, one of those notes can sell for more than ten thousand dollars.

show.label: Emperor Norton's paper money
show.sub: what one signed note can fetch at auction today

beats.say: In 1872 he even ordered a bridge built across the bay, to Oakland. People laughed. In 1936, the Bay Bridge opened.
When he died in 1880, thousands of people came to his funeral. Not bad for an emperor of one city.
Number six: Peter the Great, the tsar, or emperor, of Russia. He was about two meters tall, and full of wild energy.
In 1697, Peter went on a long trip through Western Europe. He even worked in a Dutch shipyard under a fake name.
He came home with big ideas. Russia should look modern, like Western Europe. And in Western Europe, men shaved.
So at his welcome-home party, Peter grabbed a razor and started shaving his nobles himself.
Your Majesty! My beard is sacred!
Fine. Keep it. And pay for it.
That became the beard tax. Rich merchants paid one hundred rubles a year, and got a token to prove it.

show.label: Peter's beard tax, for rich merchants
show.sub: a year, with a beard token as your receipt

beats.say: Peter also loved medicine, especially pulling teeth. He pulled them from servants and courtiers, whether they needed it or not.
Some of those teeth are still in a museum in Saint Petersburg.
So Russia's great modernizer was also its scariest dentist.

show.title: The King Who Needed the Same Four Songs

beats.say: Number five: Philip the Fifth of Spain. He was French, a grandson of King Louis the Fourteenth.
In 1700, the king of Spain died with no children, and named sixteen-year-old Philip as his heir.
But Philip suffered from deep depression. Some days he wouldn't get dressed, shave, or do any government work.
In 1724 he even quit, and handed the crown to his teenage son. Seven months later the son died, and Philip had to take the job back.
So in 1737, his wife, Queen Elisabeth, brought in Farinelli, the most famous opera singer in Europe.
What shall I sing tonight, Your Majesty?
The same four songs. Like last night.
And tomorrow?
The same four songs.
Farinelli later told the music writer Charles Burney that he sang those same four songs every night for about ten years, until the king died.

show.label: Farinelli's playlist for the king
show.sub: every night for about ten years, until 1746

beats.say: And it seems to have helped. The music calmed the king when nothing else could.
Number four: Joanna, Queen of Castile, the biggest kingdom in Spain. History calls her Joanna the Mad. That may not be fair.
She was famously in love with her husband, Philip the Handsome. Yes, that was really his nickname.
In 1506 Philip suddenly fell ill and died. He was only twenty-eight.
Joanna wouldn't let him go. That winter she set off across Castile with his coffin, heading for Granada.
The procession traveled only at night, by torchlight, and rested in monasteries during the day.
One account even says she had the coffin opened, just to see him again.
In 1509 her father, King Ferdinand, shut her away in a palace in Tordesillas. She stayed there forty-six years, until she died.

show.label: Joanna's years shut away in Tordesillas
show.sub: 1509 to 1555, while men ruled in her name

beats.say: Her father, and later her son, ruled for her. So historians still ask: was Joanna really mad, or just in the way?

show.title: The King and the Oak Tree

beats.say: Number three: King George the Third of Britain. Yes, the king who lost America.
In 1788 he became seriously ill. He talked for hours without stopping, and often didn't make sense.
His doctors were tough. One of them, Francis Willis, even tied him into a straitjacket when he wouldn't calm down.
Sit still, Your Majesty.
I am the king! I'll sit where I like!
There's a famous story that he shook hands with an oak tree, thinking it was the King of Prussia. There's no real evidence for it. It's a legend.
What's true is that he got better in 1789, and Britain held a huge thank-you service at Saint Paul's Cathedral.
But the illness came back. From 1811 his son ruled for him, and George spent his last years shut away at Windsor.
Doctors still argue about what he had. Some blame a blood disease called porphyria. Many now think it was bipolar disorder.
Number two: Ludwig the Second, King of Bavaria, in southern Germany. People called him the Fairytale King.
He became king at eighteen. He loved operas, especially Richard Wagner's, and hated politics.
So he built castles that look like opera sets: Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee, and the most famous, Neuschwanstein, started in 1869.
He also slept during the day, and took sleigh rides through the mountains at night.
One problem: he paid with his own money, and it ran out. By 1886 he owed more than fourteen million marks.
Your Majesty, the banks want their money back!
Then find me more. I'm not finished building.
In June 1886, the government declared him insane and removed him. The doctors never properly examined him.
The next evening, Ludwig and that doctor were found dead in Lake Starnberg. Nobody knows exactly what happened.
Seven weeks later, his castles opened to paying visitors. Today about one point four million people a year visit Neuschwanstein, and it inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
And number one: Charles the Sixth of France. He became king at eleven, and people called him Charles the Beloved.
In 1392, he was riding through a hot forest near Le Mans with his soldiers. He was already unwell.
A page dropped a lance with a loud clang. The king panicked, drew his sword, and attacked his own men. Several died.
From then on, he slipped in and out of serious mental illness. Sometimes he forgot his own name, and didn't recognize his wife, Queen Isabeau.
Who is that woman?
It's me, Isabeau. Your wife.
And then came the glass. A pope who lived at the time wrote this.
Sometimes he thought he was made of glass and would not let himself be touched.

show.text: Sometimes he thought he was made of glass and would not let himself be touched.
show.who: Pope Pius II, Commentaries, on King Charles VI of France

beats.say: So he had iron rods sewn into his clothes, to keep himself from breaking. Doctors call this the glass delusion, and he's one of the earliest known cases.

Sadly, France paid the price. Nobles fought for power, England invaded, and in 1420 Charles signed a treaty making England's king his heir. He ruled for forty-two years, about thirty of them while seriously ill.
So the craziest king on our list wasn't a villain. He was a sick man, stuck in a job he couldn't quit.
Honorable mention: Charles the Second of Spain. Generations of royal cousins marrying each other left him sick all his life. People said he was bewitched, and priests even tried an exorcism.
His heir, in 1700? Philip the Fifth. Small world.
So that's the list: a one-city emperor, a beard-taxing dentist, a four-song playlist, a queen and a coffin, a king and a maybe-tree, a castle addict, and a king made of glass.
Who was the most insane? Tell us in the comments.
